prompt: Bruno's Docker Desktop settings give its VM 2 GB of memory. A database container that needs 4 GB keeps failing, although his laptop has plenty of memory free. Why?
hint: Docker and Containers, lesson 5.

choices.text: The image runs under emulation for another processor, which doubles its memory
choices.why: Emulation makes an image slower, not bigger; the limit here is the VM's memory setting.

choices.text: Containers run inside Desktop's VM and never get more than it was given
choices.why: The engine and its containers live in the VM, so its memory setting is the ceiling, whatever the laptop has.

choices.text: Desktop caps every container at 2 GB unless `--memory` raises the cap
choices.why: A container has no limit until one is set; the ceiling here is the VM's size, which `--memory` cannot pass.

choices.text: The `docker` client on the laptop decides how much memory each one gets
choices.why: The client only sends requests; the engine in the VM runs the containers inside the VM's memory.

prompt: A container appends one line to a 2 GB file that came with its image. What happens in the container's filesystem?
hint: Docker and Containers, lesson 4.

choices.text: The line is written into the image's layer, and every container started from it sees it
choices.why: No container ever writes to a lower layer; the image stays as it was for every other container.

choices.text: The write is refused, since a container may not modify the layers of its image
choices.why: The read-only layer is left untouched, and the write lands on a copy in the container's own layer.

choices.text: The whole file is first copied up into the container's layer, and the copy changes
choices.why: Overlayfs never writes to a lower layer: the first write copies the file up, which here costs 2 GB.

choices.text: Just the new line goes into the upper layer, stored there as a diff against the image
choices.why: Overlayfs works on whole files, so the first write copies the entire file into the upper layer.

prompt: Two containers of the shop ended overnight. Their `lastState.terminated` shows exit code 143 for one and 137 for the other. Which reading of the two numbers is right?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lessons 19 and 35; Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6.

choices.text: 143 is the kernel's out-of-memory kill and 137 is a polite stop from the kubelet, so the first one needs a higher memory limit
choices.why: Reversed: 137 is 128 plus 9, SIGKILL, which is what the out-of-memory killer sends.

choices.text: Both are statuses the shop chose itself when it exited, so they describe what went wrong inside it, not who stopped it
choices.why: A status above 128 is a signal number plus 128; the program did not pick it.

choices.text: Both mean the liveness probe failed, because Kubernetes reports every probe failure as an exit code above 128
choices.why: A failed liveness probe ends the process with a signal, and the code names that signal, not the probe.

choices.text: 143 is SIGTERM, which the shop catches to finish its requests; 137 is SIGKILL: look at memory or the grace period
choices.why: 128 plus the signal: 15 is a polite stop, 9 is one nothing can catch.

prompt: From the pod `left` on `shop-worker`, `ping 10.244.1.2` reaches the pod `right` on `shop-worker2`, and every reply comes back with `ttl=62`. What does that number say about the path?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 18; Networks and Protocols, lesson 2.

choices.text: It left at 64, and two routers each took one off: one node, then the other
choices.why: Each node routes the packet once, and nothing hides a hop.

choices.text: The two nodes are 62 hops apart on the network that Docker created for them
choices.why: A TTL counts down from its starting value; 62 hops would leave almost nothing.

choices.text: Each veth cable takes one off, so the reply stayed inside `shop-worker2`
choices.why: A cable does not touch the TTL; only a machine that routes the packet does.

choices.text: The reply was translated twice, and every address rewrite takes one off
choices.why: There is no translation on this path; the TTL drops because the packet is routed.

prompt: One Traefik pod serves two applications on the laptop's port 8080, chosen by host name. To test the shop's route, the lesson runs `curl -s -H "Host: shop.example.test" localhost:8080/`. Why that header?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 16; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: The controller answers `404` to callers who do not identify themselves, and Host is how they do it
choices.why: The `404` was for a host no route names, not for an anonymous caller.

choices.text: The controller chooses a route by the request's Host line, and no DNS points that name at the laptop
choices.why: The address only reaches the controller; the Host line says which site is wanted.

choices.text: The header makes curl resolve `shop.example.test` through the cluster's own DNS
choices.why: A header is sent inside the request; it changes nothing about how curl looks a name up.

choices.text: Traefik routes by destination address, and the header changes the address curl connects to
choices.why: curl still connects to `localhost:8080`; both hosts arrive at the same address.

prompt: A deploy pipeline calls the API with a token from `kubectl create token deployer -n shop`. The reply is a `Status` with `"reason": "Forbidden"`, naming `system:serviceaccount:shop:deployer`, the verb `list` and the resource `pods`. What does it say, and what fixes it?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 23; Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: The namespace `shop` does not exist yet, so the API server has nowhere to look for the pods
choices.why: The account lives in `shop`, so the namespace exists; the message is about permission.

choices.text: The token was not accepted, so issue a new one with a longer `--duration`
choices.why: A token the server did not accept is a 401; this message already names the account.

choices.text: The account is known, but nothing grants it the verb; a bound Role is missing
choices.why: Authentication passed and authorisation refused: a 403, fixed with a Role and a RoleBinding.

choices.text: A rule in RBAC denies pods to service accounts, and that rule has to be deleted
choices.why: RBAC has no deny rules; anything no rule grants is refused.

prompt: A GitOps tool keeps the cluster in step with `main`. Version 1.1 shipped through a merged commit and is broken, so during the incident Carla runs `kubectl rollout undo deployment/shop`. What happens next, and what fix lasts?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lessons 35 and 39; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 4.

choices.text: The undo is right; follow it with `git reset --hard HEAD~1` and a force-push of `main`
choices.why: Reset rewrites a history other people already have; revert adds to it.

choices.text: The undo holds, because the tool reacts to new commits, and the undo came after the last one
choices.why: The tool compares the repository with the cluster on every sync, not only on new commits.

choices.text: The tool sees the undo as a new revision and commits it back to the repository for the team
choices.why: The tool pulls from git and applies; it does not write the cluster's changes back.

choices.text: The next sync brings 1.1 back from `main`; reverting it in git is what lasts
choices.why: The undo is drift, and a revert is a new commit that undoes it on the shared branch.

prompt: A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy lets a Deployment in only if every image `contains(':')` and does not end in `:latest`. Which of these images is let in although it runs whatever `latest` points to?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 25; Docker and Containers, lessons 15 and 16.

choices.text: `registry.local:5000/shop`, where the colon is the port
choices.why: There is a colon, from the registry's port, and no tag, which means `latest`.

choices.text: `registry.local:5000/shop:1.0`, since the registry has a port
choices.why: It is let in, rightly: its tag is `1.0`, an explicit version.

choices.text: `nginx:latest`, since the rule checks for the colon first
choices.why: The second half of the rule refuses an image ending in `:latest`.

choices.text: `nginx`, since a missing tag is not the text `:latest`
choices.why: It has no colon at all, so the first half of the rule refuses it.

prompt: You fix a bug and run `./build.sh` again, so `shop:1.1` on your laptop is a new image. Then `kubectl rollout restart deployment/shop`. The new pods still behave like the old build. Why?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 1; Docker and Containers, lesson 16.

choices.text: A rollout restart reuses the old containers rather than making new pods
choices.why: It replaces the pods with new ones from the same template, as an update would.

choices.text: Each node keeps the `shop:1.1` it was given, and a tag already there is not pulled again
choices.why: The nodes have their own image store; `kind load docker-image` hands them the new build.

choices.text: Docker on the laptop keeps the old image under that tag until somebody runs `docker image prune`
choices.why: The rebuild moved the tag on the laptop; the stale copy is on the nodes.

choices.text: The ReplicaSet pins the old digest, and the tag `latest` would force a fresh pull
choices.why: `latest` is only a name; it would not put the laptop's build inside the nodes either.

prompt: `shop-worker2` turns `NotReady`, and `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` lists no kubelet pod whose logs you could read. Where do you look for the kubelet's own account?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 4; Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5.

choices.text: In `kubectl logs` of the node's kube-proxy pod, which runs the kubelet beside it as a sidecar
choices.why: kube-proxy is a DaemonSet pod started by the kubelet, not a home for it.

choices.text: In etcd, under `/registry/pods`, where every kubelet writes the lines it logs
choices.why: etcd holds objects written through the API server, not anybody's log.

choices.text: On the node, with `systemctl status kubelet` and `journalctl -u kubelet`, because it is a service
choices.why: The kubelet runs pods, so it cannot be one: systemd starts it like any daemon.

choices.text: In `/etc/kubernetes/manifests` on that node, where its static pod file has been removed
choices.why: That directory holds the control plane's static pods, which the kubelet itself runs.

prompt: On the kind cluster, `kubectl get nodes -o wide` shows the OS image `Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie)` and the kernel `6.18.44-fc-v70 (amd64)` on all three nodes. Why is the kernel the same on every node?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 5; Docker and Containers, lesson 2.

choices.text: Debian 13 ships that kernel release, so every Debian node reports it
choices.why: An image named after a distribution brings its files, not its kernel.

choices.text: The kubelet reports the control plane's kernel for every node it lists
choices.why: Each node reports its own, and here the three are one kernel.

choices.text: kind copies one kernel image into each node when it builds the cluster
choices.why: A kind node brings files, not a kernel; there is no kernel inside the image to copy.

choices.text: The nodes are containers, and containers run on the host's kernel
choices.why: So the column shows the laptop's own kernel, which is why the nodes start in seconds.

prompt: Bruno committed his `~/.kube/config` to the team's repository and pushed it. A day later he deleted it in a new commit and added it to `.gitignore`. What does the situation still need?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 7; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.

choices.text: Replacing the credentials in it, because the key stays in the history as an admin's key
choices.why: A committed secret is public from that moment; only revoking it fixes anything.

choices.text: Switching everybody to a new context with `use-context`, so the old entries stop working
choices.why: A context is a local pointer in the file; changing it revokes nothing on the server.

choices.text: Nothing more: the deleting commit removed the file, and the ignore rule keeps it out
choices.why: The old commit still holds it, in every clone and on the shared copy.

choices.text: The cluster side is fine, since a kubeconfig holds addresses rather than credentials
choices.why: It holds a working client certificate and key; reading it makes you an administrator.

prompt: A service needs about thirty seconds after start before `/healthz` answers. Its only probe is liveness, `periodSeconds: 5` and `failureThreshold: 3`, and the pod keeps restarting and never serves. What fixes it without slowing hang detection later?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 22.

choices.text: `restartPolicy: OnFailure`, so a failed probe is not counted as a crash
choices.why: A liveness failure restarts the container under either policy; the probe still fires too early.

choices.text: A startup probe allowing a full minute, then liveness takes over as before
choices.why: Liveness and readiness wait until the startup probe has succeeded once.

choices.text: A liveness `failureThreshold` of 12, which gives a minute before any restart
choices.why: That minute would also apply to every real hang, for the rest of the pod's life.

choices.text: A readiness probe instead of liveness, since readiness restarts no container
choices.why: The restarts stop, and so does any restart when the process really hangs.

prompt: `team-a` has a ResourceQuota of `pods: "4"`. `kubectl scale deployment shop --replicas=6 -n team-a` succeeds, the Deployment then reads `4/6`, and no pod is `Pending`. Where is the reason written?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 20.

choices.text: In the kubelet's log on the node that ran out of room for pods
choices.why: No node was involved; the quota is checked by the API server on every create.

choices.text: In a `FailedScheduling` event on the fifth pod, written by the scheduler
choices.why: No fifth pod exists to schedule; it was refused before it was stored.

choices.text: In a `FailedCreate` event on the ReplicaSet the quota turned away
choices.why: The ReplicaSet tried to create the fifth pod, and the quota turned it away.

choices.text: In the output of the scale command, printed as a warning nobody read
choices.why: The scale was accepted: it only changed a number on the Deployment.

prompt: On the laptop's cluster, `kube-scheduler.yaml` is moved out of `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`, and then the Deployment `shop` is scaled from one replica to three. Which of these happen? Choose all that apply.
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 4.

choices.text: The pod that was already running keeps serving
choices.why: It already has a node, and its kubelet keeps it running.

choices.text: Two new pods are created, and they wait in `Pending`
choices.why: The two controllers did their part; nobody chose a node.

choices.text: The scale command is refused until a scheduler returns
choices.why: The API server accepts it; only the step of choosing a node is missing.

choices.text: The scale has to be repeated once the file is back
choices.why: The work waits in the API server, and the new scheduler places both pods.

prompt: The shop's manifests live in a git repository, and after an eventful week `kubectl apply -k shop` is run from it. Which hand-made changes does that apply undo? Choose all that apply.
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lessons 7, 35, 38 and 39.

choices.text: `replicas` raised to 5 with `kubectl scale` during an incident
choices.why: The file says otherwise, and apply makes the live object match it.

choices.text: The image moved back a revision with `kubectl rollout undo`
choices.why: The repository still names the newer image, so apply brings it back.

choices.text: A Deployment `debug` made with `kubectl create`, in no file
choices.why: Apply changes what the files describe and never deletes anything else.

choices.text: An old generated ConfigMap the overlay stopped producing
choices.why: Apply leaves it in place; removing it is a prune, which plain apply does not do.

prompt: `~/iac-env.sh` exports the variables that point the lab's command-line tools at its local emulator. In a new terminal Ana runs `sh ~/iac-env.sh`, and `env` then lists none of them. In that terminal, the line that works is `___ ~/iac-env.sh`.
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 1; Linux and the Command Line, lesson 9.

prompt: A colleague's first commit of a new Terraform configuration holds `main.tf`, `versions.tf` and the whole `.terraform/` directory, all 789M of it, and leaves out `.terraform.lock.hcl`. What should that commit hold instead?
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 2; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.

choices.text: The `.tf` files and `.terraform/`, so that nobody has to run `init` again
choices.why: `.terraform/` holds a downloaded provider that `init` fetches again; like `node_modules/`, it stays out of Git.

choices.text: Only the `.tf` files: the lock file and `.terraform/` are both rebuilt
choices.why: Without the lock file, two people running `init` a week apart can get two provider versions.

choices.text: All of it: the `.tf` files, `.terraform/` and the lock file together
choices.why: The lock file belongs in Git; the provider directory is a download `init` repeats, and 789M in every clone.

choices.text: The `.tf` files and the lock file, with `.terraform/` in `.gitignore`

prompt: Ana's `network` variable carries the rule `can(cidrsubnet(var.network.cidr, 8, 2))`, and subnet `a` takes `cidrsubnet(var.network.cidr, 8, 1)`. A colleague passes `cidr = "10.20.0.0/20"` for a smaller VPC. What happens?

prompt: Ana makes two subnets with `for_each`, then ties each to a route table with `for_each = toset(values(aws_subnet.app)[*].id)`. The first plan stops with `Invalid for_each argument`. What is wrong, and what fixes it?

prompt: Two applies against the shop's remote backend both sit at the confirmation question. One is stopped with Ctrl+C; the other gets `kill -9` when its CI runner is reclaimed. Which one leaves a `.tflock` object behind that blocks the next run?

choices.text: The interrupted one, which keeps its lock in case the apply resumes

choices.text: Neither: the backend deletes a lock object once the process that wrote it is gone
choices.why: S3 knows nothing about the process; the object stays until somebody deletes it, which is why `force-unlock` exists.

choices.text: The killed one: `SIGKILL` cannot be caught, so its lock is never deleted
choices.why: A process cannot clean up after `KILL`, and the lock object stays until `force-unlock` removes it.

choices.text: Rotate the secret, and treat the leaked value as public from now on

choices.text: Nothing: the new commit took the file out of the repository's history

choices.text: Mark the variable `sensitive = true`, so the old commit hides its value

prompt: The lesson's pipeline reaches the cloud account through two roles, `shop-plan` and `shop-apply`, and stores no access key anywhere. Which statements about them hold? Choose all that apply.

prompt: The shop's budget counts only spending tagged `Project = shop`, which `default_tags` puts on everything the configuration creates. Bruno made a 100 GB volume by hand for an export and forgot it. Which statement is right?

prompt: A CloudFormation stack is being created, and the API refuses one of its resources halfway through. How does that end differ from a Terraform apply that fails the same way?

choices.why: Terraform cannot: each resource is its own API call, and what succeeded stays in the state.

choices.text: Terraform rolls back what it made; the stack keeps it for later

prompt: `ansible web1 -m command -a "dpkg -l | grep -c ^ii"` fails, with `dpkg-query` saying that no packages match `|`, `-c` and `^ii`. Run with `-m shell` against both web servers, the same line prints `193` for each. Why the difference?

choices.text: `command` always reports CHANGED, and Ansible counts that as a failure

choices.text: `command` runs it with no shell, so the pipe reaches `dpkg` as arguments
choices.why: A pipe is set up by a shell; the `shell` module puts `/bin/sh` in front, and the line means what it says.

choices.why: `dpkg -l` reads as any user; an error naming `|` and `-c` as packages is a parsing problem.

choices.text: `grep` is missing on `web1`, and the `shell` module carries its own copy
choices.why: `grep` is installed; `dpkg` even listed the `grep` package when it was handed that word.

prompt: At 03:40 the engineer on call ends an outage by editing nginx's configuration by hand on a web server, and writes nothing into any description. Which statements hold? Choose all that apply.
hint: Infrastructure as Code, lesson 19.

choices.text: With a Puppet agent at its defaults, the edit is undone within half an hour
choices.why: `runinterval` is 1800 seconds; the next run finds a difference and writes the file as described.

choices.text: With Ansible run from a laptop, the edit stays until the playbook runs again
choices.why: With push, nothing compares the machine until the next run, which may be tomorrow or never.

choices.text: A Puppet agent keeps the edit, as it can tell an outage fix from a mistake
choices.why: It undoes both with the same confidence, because it has no way to tell them apart.

choices.text: An agent rewrites the file only if the description changed since its last run
choices.why: Every run compares the machine with the description, so a hand edit alone is a difference.

prompt: A container runs from `shop-web:1.2.0`, and somebody fixes the page with `docker exec`, writing into `/var/www/html/index.html`; `curl` shows the fix. Later the container is removed and started again from the same image. What does `curl` show, and where should the fix have gone?

choices.text: No page at all, since removing the container deleted the image's files
choices.why: Removal deletes only the container's layer, and a new container is the image again.

choices.text: The image's own page; the fix belongs in the template, as a new version
choices.why: The edit lived in the container's writable layer, which went away with the container.

choices.text: The fixed page, since `docker exec` wrote into the image it came from
choices.why: `exec` writes into the container's own layer; the image stays exactly as it was built.

prompt: loanbook's server builds its image as `localhost/loanbook` with no tag, and the unit file starts `Image=localhost/loanbook:latest`. Next month a new build goes out and the page breaks. What does that naming cost Ana at that moment?

choices.why: A container start pulls only when the name is missing on the machine, and `localhost/` names no registry.

choices.text: Nothing: the git tag `v0.3.0` travels into the image, so the old build is found by it
choices.why: A git tag names a commit, not an image; nothing copied it onto the build.

choices.text: The unit no longer starts, since Quadlet wants a real version number in place of `latest`
choices.why: The unit started with `:latest` in lesson 15; the name is accepted, it just says nothing.

choices.text: No way back by name: `latest` names what is there now, never what ran before
choices.why: That is the first cost of `latest`: a rollback needs the name of the previous build.

prompt: To test from laptop without going through Caddy, a colleague changes loanbook's unit to `PublishPort=8000:8000`. What has that changed on srv?

choices.why: With no address in front, the door is on the network card too, and Caddy stops being the only way in.

choices.text: Laptop now reaches it over HTTPS on port 8000, since Caddy's certificate covers the whole host
choices.why: The certificate is Caddy's, on Caddy's port; port 8000 answers the app directly, unencrypted.

choices.text: Nothing outside srv changes, since Caddy is still the one door the configuration names
choices.why: The Caddyfile is untouched, but the container now has a second door that bypasses it.

choices.text: Caddy can no longer reach the app, because a port is published on a single address
choices.why: Every address includes the loopback one; Caddy still gets through. What changed is who else does.

prompt: Every future deploy of loanbook replaces its container with one built from a new image. Why does the unit keep the SQLite file in the named volume `loanbook-data` rather than inside the container?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15; Docker and Containers, lesson 7.

choices.text: SQLite inside a container writes into the image, and the image is read-only
choices.why: Writes inside a container go to its writable layer, which exists exactly as long as the container.

choices.text: A container's writable layer is removed with it, and the volume outlives every container
choices.why: So a replaced container takes its own layer away, and the loans stay in the volume.

choices.text: A named volume lets Caddy read the database file directly whenever it answers a request for the list
choices.why: Caddy only forwards requests to port 8000; it never touches the database.

choices.text: Without a volume, `Restart=always` would have nothing to bring back after the program crashes
choices.why: Restarting works on any container; the volume decides what data survives, not whether it restarts.

prompt: A reviewer reads loanbook's Containerfile and asks why it has `USER 1000`, when the container already has walls around it. Which answer agrees with both lessons?

choices.text: Podman refuses to start an image whose process would run as root, so the line is required
choices.why: Nothing refused it: an image with no `USER` runs as root by default, which is the problem.

choices.text: A bug in the program, or a flaw past the walls, then acts as an ordinary user rather than as root
choices.why: The walls stay either way; what changes is how much a single mistake is worth.

choices.text: It makes the image smaller, because the files root would need are left out of the build
choices.why: `USER` changes who the process runs as; it adds and removes no files.

prompt: From laptop, `curl -sS https://loans.lab/healthz` answers `curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate`. Caddy issued the certificate with `tls internal`. What is the fix both lessons agree on?

choices.text: Configure Caddy to send the full chain, because an intermediate certificate is missing from what it sends

choices.text: Add `-k` to the curl command, since this is a lab that nobody else can reach
choices.why: Telling the client not to check removes the one thing that tells a real server from an impostor.

choices.text: Copy Caddy's local root to laptop, read what it is, and add it to the trust store
choices.why: Laptop then trusts that one authority on purpose, and the same request succeeds.

prompt: loanbook moves to `loans.example.org` on a public server, and the Caddyfile loses its `tls internal` line. Why could the lab's way of making HTTPS work not simply be kept?

choices.text: Visitors trust the roots already in their stores, and Caddy's local root is on laptop alone
choices.why: A public authority's root is already on the visitors' machines, which is why the line goes.

choices.text: A public name does not go in `/etc/hosts`, and Caddy's own authority signs the names listed there
choices.why: The hosts file only told laptop where `loans.lab` was; it has nothing to do with who signs.

choices.text: Public authorities refuse to deal with a server whose local authority is still switched on
choices.why: The reason is on the visitor's side: nobody else installed that root, and nobody should.

choices.text: The lab's local root expires within a year, and a public site would break along with it
choices.why: The capture shows that root valid until 2036; the trouble is who trusts it, not how long it lasts.

prompt: On laptop, `curl -sS https://loans.lab/healthz` prints `{"ok": true}`, but `dig +short loans.lab` prints nothing at all. What explains the two answers?

choices.text: The record has not propagated yet, and dig will agree with curl once the old answer's TTL runs out

choices.why: It accepts pushes to any branch; the trouble was only what a clone checks out.

prompt: In a design question about your deployed project, the interviewer asks how you would make it survive a data-centre failure. You have never built that. Which answer follows lesson 14 and is also true to the cloud lesson?

choices.text: The provider keeps a cloud server running for me, so the project already survives a data-centre failure
choices.why: A confident answer that is wrong: an instance lives in one zone, and goes down with it.

choices.text: I haven't built it. An instance lives in one zone, so I'd try two zones behind a load balancer, in a lab
choices.why: Plain about the edge, what is known nearby, and how it would be found out.

choices.text: I'd add a second copy in another zone of the same building, which costs nothing extra on the bill
choices.why: Zones are separate datacentres, and the second copy is paid for every hour.

choices.text: I don't know; that is a question for seniors, so I'd rather move on and talk about my tests instead

choices.text: One server running the service, its parts named, and where it breaks first

choices.text: The cluster, because interviewers read Kubernetes as the mark of a serious design

prompt: Your first task at work is a one-line fix to the team's deploy script. Which of these make it finished properly, the way the portfolio course practised? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A commit message that says what changed, and why it had to change
choices.why: The diff shows what; only the message can say why.

choices.text: Folding in the two unrelated tidy-ups you noticed in the same file
choices.why: Each goes in its own change; three unrelated fixes in one are harder to review than three apart.

choices.text: Reading your own diff before you ask anybody to review it
choices.why: A self-review finds the slips before a colleague has to.

choices.text: Holding it back until it can be shown with a larger second task
choices.why: The first thing shipped should be visible as soon as it is done, as the normal end of a task.

prompt: A take-home for a junior cloud role suggests about three hours. At three hours your configuration builds the network, and the test you planned is not written. What does lesson 13 say to do?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 13.

choices.text: Stop, and say in the note what is missing and what you would do with more time
choices.why: The reviewer is also checking how you behave with a deadline.

choices.text: Ask for two more days, because a late and finished submission beats an incomplete one
choices.why: A late, perfect submission is usually worse than an on-time, incomplete one.

choices.text: Keep going until the test exists, since a complete submission is what gets graded
choices.why: A submission that obviously took twice the time says you did not read the brief or cannot estimate.

choices.text: Hand it in without mentioning the test, so it is judged only on what is there
choices.why: Silence about a gap reads worse than naming it; the note is where the missing pieces go.

prompt: In a live exercise you are given a web server's log and asked to count each status code. Which plan, said aloud before typing, follows lesson 12 and would also give the right counts?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 12; Linux and the Command Line, lesson 8.

choices.text: I'll cut out the status column and use `sort -u`, which gives each status with its count
choices.why: `sort -u` drops the duplicates and prints no counts at all.

choices.text: I'll cut out the status column, sort it, count runs with `uniq -c`, then `sort -rn` the counts
choices.why: The plan comes first, and `sort` before `uniq` is what makes the counts right.

choices.text: I'll cut out the status column and pipe it straight into `uniq -c`, then sort the counts
choices.why: `uniq` collapses only adjacent lines, so unsorted input gives wrong counts that look right.

choices.text: I'll start typing `uniq -c` at once and explain it afterwards, since a pipeline on screen speaks for itself
choices.why: The interviewer can only follow thinking that is said, and the plan is the step that lets them stop you.

choices.text: A certification first, since every employer filters on one for these roles
